D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment
Enables VLMs as Zero-Shot Robotic Reward Models

Marius Memmel Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: NVIDIA, *Equal Contribution    Shawn Yin Affiliation: University of Washington    Urvi Rutia Affiliation: University of Washington    Angad Wadhwa Affiliation: University of Washington    Eldon Li Affiliation: University of Washington    Gavin Angeloff Affiliation: University of Washington    Ankit Goyal Affiliation: NVIDIA, *Equal Contribution    Jesse Zhang Affiliation: University of Washington    Dieter Fox Affiliation: University of Washington    Fabio Ramos Affiliation: NVIDIA, *Equal Contribution    Anqi Li Affiliation: NVIDIA, *Equal Contribution Affiliation: Equal Advising    Abhishek Gupta Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: Equal Advising
Abstract

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) hold promise for zero-shot video task-progress estimation in robot learning, yet existing frameworks frequently suffer from confirmation bias, hallucinating progress in failed executions due to implicit success assumptions or relative temporal ranking designs. Naïve prompting of frontier models collapses into a binary success detector that fails to capture nuanced, non-linear progress and failures. While post-training approaches can mitigate this through explicit training, they demand expensive real-world robotics data and require computationally intensive post-training for every individual base model. To resolve these limitations, we introduce D&A (Describe & Assess): our approach decouples progress estimation into an objective, task-grounded textual description of scene dynamics followed by an assessment phase using explicit rubrics. By compelling the VLM to synthesize an explicit, text-based definition of absolute success before scoring, the framework anchors evaluations to an external, global criterion rather than the video’s internal timeline. Empirical results demonstrate that our method calibrates zero-shot estimates and mitigates confirmation bias, providing fine-grained, partial progress metrics that accurately penalize failed executions while correctly interpolating successful runs. Being purely prompt-based, D&A generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and benchmarks—matching or surpassing post-trained reward models—and its reward estimates enable efficient downstream reinforcement learning.

Website at https://weirdlabuw.github.io/dna

I Introduction

First impressions are notoriously difficult to overcome [1]. When evaluating complex situations, humans often exhibit confirmation bias [2], seeking and interpreting evidence that aligns with their initial hypotheses and introducing systematic errors into judgment. Similar biases appear in language models, which, trained to appear competent to human evaluators, distort answers to agree with users or take “shortcuts” to appear to solve given tasks [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Crucially, the psychology literature shows such biases can be mitigated through structured procedures that mandate a comprehensive description of the available data before any task assessment [9, 10].

We build on this intuition to design better robotics reward models for downstream applications, e.g., real-world reinforcement learning and failure explanation. When naïvely querying Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for zero-shot video reward estimation, we observe these same confirmation-bias shortcuts: the models frequently hallucinate progress even when little to no meaningful advancement has occurred (see Fig. 1). Current zero-shot robotics reward models fall victim to the same issue—frameworks like GVL [11] and TOPReward [12] estimate progress by ranking shuffled video frames or tracking token logits—our experiments show that these approaches bias towards task success. For downstream reinforcement or imitation learning algorithms, these erroneous evaluations become highly misleading reward signals that severely impede policy learning.

To bypass the limitations of zero-shot foundation models, recent approaches post-train models on task-specific robotic datasets [13, 14, 15, 16]. Yet diverse real-world robotics data, with labeled failures, is hard to obtain [17], limiting the generalization capabilities of the resulting models. Post-training is further limited to smaller, less capable open-source models and must be repeated for each individual base VLM, creating a cost, compute, and capability barrier to truly generalist robotics reward models.

Instead, we propose D&A (Describe & Assess), a zero-shot reward model that avoids the bias issues of prior zero-shot methods while achieving better visual and semantic generalization than post-trained reward models. Being zero-shot is central to its effectiveness: requiring no robotics-specific training, the same prompt-based recipe drops directly onto any promptable VLM and improves for free as the underlying models advance. D&A decouples evaluation into two distinct stages, description and assessment. It first forces the VLM to generate an explicit, textual description of what the robot actually did, inducing an objective foundation for progress measurement. It then assesses progress by reasoning about what task success means semantically and anchoring its reward estimate to the success criterion. Conditioned on the trajectory description and this success reasoning, the VLM predicts progress over key frames in [0,1][0,1] as dense rewards for policy learning. We further show that this paradigm can be easily adapted to generate rich natural language feedback that goes beyond binary reward signals and provides targeted corrective context for policy improvement.

In summary, D&A is a reward model paradigm that decouples video description from progress assessment, enabling zero-shot robotics reward modeling with pre-trained VLMs. Because it is purely prompt-based, D&A is model-agnostic and requires no robotics data or fine-tuning; it generalizes across tasks, embodiments, and language, matching or outperforming post-trained models on reward benchmarks. Our scaling experiments show D&A improves with VLM capability across four model families and 28 open- and closed-source models. On real-world online and offline reinforcement learning with a DROID Franka and two bimanual YAM arm tasks, D&A improves success rate over both zero-shot and post-trained reward models by +95%+95\%, +15%+15\%, and +45%+45\%, respectively. Finally, scaling up D&A to GPT-6 Astra achieves SOTA performance on D&A-Bench, RBM-EVAL-OOD, and RoboRewardBenchmark, surpassing all seven pre-trained and zero-shot baselines.

II Related Work

Foundation models as reward models. LLMs and VLMs have been widely used to specify rewards, e.g., by generating executable reward code or shaping terms from natural language [18, 19, 20, 21], but such methods typically assume access to privileged low-dimensional state that is unavailable in real-world deployment. A more deployable alternative uses pre-trained VLMs as zero-shot progress or success estimators directly from pixels [22, 23, 24, 11, 12, 25]. D&A belongs to this zero-shot family, but whereas prior methods extract a scalar signal directly—e.g., ranking shuffled frames in GVL [11] or reading the logit of a “True” token in TOPReward [12]—we route reward estimation through explicit description and assess phases, which we find essential for countering the success bias of direct prompting.

Post-trained reward models. To improve reliability, a growing line of work fine-tunes VLMs and VLAs on robotics data with progress-prediction objectives [13, 15, 16, 14, 26, 27, 28] or language reasoning [29, 30]. RoboReward [15] predicts discretized progress labels obtained via counterfactual instruction relabeling, while Robometer [16] jointly predicts progress, success, and trajectory preferences from a large curated dataset. These models inherit the cost of collecting diverse, high-quality robot data [17], are restricted to open-source backbones, and must be retrained as stronger base models appear. D&A instead remains fully zero-shot, making it model-agnostic and improving with frontier VLM improvements, while matching or exceeding post-trained models on out-of-distribution benchmarks.

III Demonstrating Bias in Zero-Shot VLM Prompting

We begin with a qualitative example showing that directly prompting a zero-shot VLM [31] for per-frame progress—conditioned on a robot video and its task instruction—fails to produce accurate rewards. Given an expert demonstration paired with the correct instruction, VLMs generally produce reasonable per-frame [0,1][0,1] rewards that end at 1.01.0. However, when the robot performs the task incorrectly or suboptimally, they often “shortcut” by assuming success—precisely the case a reward model must detect to correct a deployed policy.

For example, in Fig. 2 we prompt GPT-5.3 with “provide per-timestep rewards for this video of a robot ‘unfolding the shirt’.” However, the video (from the π0\pi_{0}-FAST blog [32]) in fact shows a π0\pi_{0} policy folding a shirt. Rather than reasoning about task completion, the model writes a reward function that scores normalized mean pixel differences between consecutive frames, rewarding motion rather than progress. This reflects a confirmation bias arising from fine-tuning on human feedback, which makes models unlikely to challenge user assumptions [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].

While prompt engineering can mitigate specific cases, our experiments (Sec. V) show that existing zero-shot reward methods—built on both closed- and open-source VLMs with custom prompting and reward-extraction schemes—still perform poorly across benchmarks, real-world tasks, and embodiments. Next, we detail our solution: decoupled description and assessment phases.

IV D&A: Decoupling Description and Assessment

Problem Formulation. Given an image sequence (video) o1:T≔{o1,o2,…,oT}o_{1:T}\coloneqq\{o_{1},o_{2},\ldots,o_{T}\} of length TT of a robot performing a task specified by natural language instruction ll, our goal is to predict a corresponding sequence of reward values r1:T≔{r1,r2,…,rT}r_{1:T}\coloneqq\{r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{T}\}. Each scalar value rt∈[0,1]r_{t}\in[0,1] represents the estimated reward at timestep tt, where rt=0r_{t}=0 indicates no progress and rt=1r_{t}=1 corresponds to task completion. We construct a mapping function R:(o1:T,l)↦r1:TR:(o_{1:T},\,l)\mapsto r_{1:T} that estimates rewards from the multi-modal inputs o1:To_{1:T} and ll. Prior works either post-train a VLM to learn RR [13, 14, 15, 16], directly query a VLM with a custom prompt and shuffled image inputs [11, 33], or produce r1:Tr_{1:T} by inspecting the logits of a specific token after processing o1:T,lo_{1:T},l [12].

Method Overview. We would like to directly use pre-trained VLMs, zero-shot, for reward prediction; doing so allows us to leverage the generalization capabilities and learned reasoning chains of ever-improving frontier VLMs trained on internet-scale data, all without the tedium of robotics-specific post-training. But in practice, as demonstrated in Sec. III, we find that naïvely instantiating R(o1:T,l)R(o_{1:T},l) as a VLM suffers from confirmation bias, where the model predicts increasing rewards regardless of whether the observation-language pairing represents a success or failure. To address these limitations, we propose Describe and Assess (D&A), which decomposes RR into two components with an explicit natural-language interface:

Describerd1:T=D(o1:T),⊳​Describes observed behavior in languageAssessorr1:T=A(l,d1:T).⊳​Scores behavior against description\begin{array}[]{lll}\text{Describer}&d_{1:T}=D(o_{1:T}),&\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{\vartriangleright\text{Describes observed behavior in language}}\\ \text{Assessor}&r_{1:T}=A(l,d_{1:T}).&\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}{\vartriangleright\text{Scores behavior against description}}\\ \end{array}

 (1)

Both functions can use the same VLM (or another function with the same specification) but are specified by different inputs and prompts and have no shared context. Each function has a specific task to help prevent inherent VLM biases that can contaminate reward generation. The full reward function is the composition R(o1:T,l)=A(l,D(o1:T))R(o_{1:T},l)=A\big(l,\,D(o_{1:T})\big). While we use o1:To_{1:T} notation here, in practice, we linearly downsample the TT frames to HH frames with H≪TH\ll T, e.g., H=8H=8, and then linearly interpolate the rewards to length TT to reduce inference cost and time. We detail the describer next in Sec. IV-A, followed by the assessor in Sec. IV-B. We provide a visual overview of D&A in Fig. 3.

IV-A Describing the Robot Trajectory Video

The role of the describer D(o1:T)D(o_{1:T}) is to describe what the robot has accomplished in o1:To_{1:T} unconditioned on the task instruction ll. Withholding ll avoids confirmation bias [2, 3]: a describer that knows the intended task tends to narrate behavior as if that task were being accomplished, regardless of what occurred. See Fig. 3 for an example description.

Describing the full trajectory at once. In contrast to prior work [13, 14, 15, 16, 26] that predicts a single reward rt=R(o1:t,l)r_{t}=R(o_{1:t},l) causally and then iterates over tt to label dense rewards, D&A consumes the entire trajectory o1:To_{1:T} in a single pass. By describing the trajectory holistically, DD can place each timestep in the context of what happens before and after it, yielding descriptions that are temporally consistent.

Grounding the description in scene entities. Withholding ll avoids confirmation bias but introduces a new failure mode: without any knowledge of the task, the describer may omit details that turn out to be critical for downstream assessment. Take the example in Fig. 3, where an entity extractor may describe the target book as “Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahnemann, “the book with an orange spine”, “the book with a pencil on the white cover”, etc. The entity should reflect the granularity in the instruction to avoid ambiguity in the description. To resolve this without leaking ll into the describer, we decompose DD into two stages: an entity extractor EE that lists all scene entities ee, both task-relevant and task-irrelevant, from the instruction and video, and a grounded describer DdescD^{\text{desc}} that narrates the trajectory anchored to those entities: d1:T=Ddesc(o1:T,E(o1:T,l))d_{1:T}=D^{\text{desc}}\big(o_{1:T},\,E(o_{1:T},l)\big). Since DdescD^{\text{desc}} does not know which entities are task-relevant, the full describer DD is effectively blind to ll. Next, we describe how the description is used by the assessor.

IV-B Success Criteria Generation and Reward Assessment

Given the grounded description dd and instruction ll, the assessor’s role is to produce the per-timestep reward sequence r1:Tr_{1:T}. At this stage, one might again be tempted to naïvely query an LLM/VLM directly by giving it (l,d)(l,d) and asking it to score progress. In practice, however, we find this naïve version fails in a characteristic way: the assessor frequently collapses to outputting all zeros (when it cannot tell whether meaningful progress has been made) or becomes a binary success detector and simply interpolates from 00 to 11 as shown in Fig. 1. However, to generate rewards useful for downstream applications, we would want them to encode much more granular progress information, e.g., partial progress towards task or subtask completions. Such granular rewards would provide more useful, dense signals for policy learning, e.g., by improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning policies or by helping to filter out poor-quality actions in imitation learning [34].

Grounding the assessor in an explicit success criterion. This failure mode suggests the assessor lacks a clear target for progress: ll specifies what to do, but not necessarily what describes task success. We address this by having the assessor first produce task completion explicitly. Concretely, given (l,d1:T)(l,d_{1:T}), the assessor internally generates a natural-language success criterion cc—a description of the observable state of the world when ll has been fully accomplished—and then scores each timestep of the description against cc rather than against ll alone: r1:T=A(l,d1:T)=Ascore(d1:T,C(l,d1:T)),r_{1:T}=A(l,\,d_{1:T})=A^{\text{score}}\big(d_{1:T},\,C(l,\,d_{1:T})\big), where CC generates the success criterion cc and AscoreA^{\text{score}} scores the description against it. Anchoring assessment to cc reframes “estimate progress toward ll” as the better-posed question “how close is dd to satisfying success criteria cc?”, helping (1) admit a meaningful notion of partial progress and (2) resist both reward collapse modes. In practice, criterion generation and scoring occur within the single assessor call AA via system prompting: the model is instructed to first articulate the success condition for ll, then score each timestep of dd relative to it—forcing an implicit rubric [35] design through CoT reasoning [36]. See Fig. 3 for an example.

IV-C From Progress to Rich Language Feedback

Scalar reward signals execution failure without offering actionable context for policy correction. By evaluating trajectory progress relative to defined success criteria, D&A constructs an implicit semantic rubric over time. Tracking criteria fulfillment across timesteps enables D&A to localize execution deviations, demonstrating an implicit understanding of how and why a trajectory failed. To convert these diagnostic capabilities into downstream guidance, we augment the assessor AA with a feedback generator F(l,d1:T)F(l,d_{1:T}) that outputs a text string ff containing a failure analysis and corrective instructions. This updates the assessor formulation to: A(l,d1:T)=Ascore(d1:T,C(l,d1:T),F(l,d1:T))A(l,d_{1:T})=A^{\text{score}}\big(d_{1:T},C(l,d_{1:T}),F(l,d_{1:T})\big). See Fig. 3 for feedback examples.

IV-D Using D&A for Downstream Policy Improvement

The dense progress rewards and rich language feedback produced by D&A can be readily leveraged across various downstream policy improvement paradigms. Here we outline how D&A accelerates the paradigms used in our experiments in Sec. V, online and offline reinforcement learning (RL) and Code-as-Policies (CaP) [37]. Though we specifically detail those, D&A is a general-purpose reward and rich feedback framework and can be paired with other applications.

Online RL. In online RL, the agent improves its behavior through active interaction with the environment. Here, the absolute progress score r1:T=R(o1:T,l)r_{1:T}=R(o_{1:T},l) from D&A serves directly as the dense environment reward and can be optimized by any online RL algorithm. In our experiments, we fine-tune a frozen base policy with latent-space RL [38].

Offline RL. In offline RL, we are given a dataset 𝒟={τn}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\{\tau_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} of trajectories without ground-truth reward labels, and use D&A to supply the missing reward signal. Since D&A’s progress scores are bounded within [0,1][0,1] and reflect global task completion, we treat them as a potential function [39], from which we derive per-timestep potential-based dense rewards rtr_{t} and, in turn, offline advantages: At=rm​i​n​(t+C,T)−rtA_{t}=r_{min(t+C,T)}-r_{t} with action chunk size CC. We use these advantages for filtering the training data or conditioning a policy on them (cf. RECAP and CFGRL [27, 40]); at test time, conditioning on a positive advantage biases generation towards optimal trajectories, maximizing downstream performance using D&A’s zero-shot rewards.

Code-as-Policies. Recent observations in robot failure analysis [41] and feedback-driven optimization [42] suggest that rich language feedback can improve policy performance. We evaluate D&A as a between-attempt feedback source for an open-loop CaP planner. At every attempt, the planner observes the initial scene state and generates a code plan which is then executed open-loop in the environment. Across attempts, the planner keeps track of previous plans, and feedback generated by D&A which identifies the failure modes and proposes corrections.

V Experimental Evaluation

Our evaluation aims to address the following questions:

  1. (Q1)

    Effectiveness: Is D&A an effective reward model for real-world offline and online RL?

  2. (Q2)

    Generalization: How well does D&A generalize to different tasks and embodiments?

  3. (Q3)

    Scaling: How does D&A scale with the underlying VLM?

  4. (Q4)

    Ablation and analysis: What components contribute to D&A’s performance?

  5. (Q5)

    Rich feedback: Can rich feedback generated by D&A improve over scalar rewards?

We evaluate D&A against the six strongest-performing approaches, spanning both explicitly post-trained and zero-shot reward models to provide a comprehensive analysis of the current landscape. If not denoted otherwise, we choose Gemini 3 Flash as a base model for D&A to balance cost and performance, but also report benchmark numbers for GPT-6 Astra (D&A∗) to demonstrate capability scaling.

Post-trained Baselines are explicitly trained on robotics datasets to predict progress. The following approaches all use Qwen-3-VL [43] as the base model. RoboReward [15] fine-tunes to predict discrete end-of-episode scores from 1 to 5, trained on large-scale robotic data [44, 45] augmented with counterfactual language instructions that simulate failed or mismatched trajectories. Robometer [16] fine-tunes on RBM-1M (optimal and suboptimal data) with a multi-objective framework that jointly predicts continuous progress in [0,1][0,1], binary success, and pairwise trajectory preferences. SOLE-R1 [30] fine-tunes on CoT [36] and continuous progress estimates and then uses reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) to further tune the model.

Zero-shot Baselines leverage the world knowledge of off-the-shelf VLMs without any task- or robotics-specific fine-tuning. Naive VLM models the mapping R:(o1:T,l)↦r1:TR:(o_{1:T},\,l)\mapsto r_{1:T} with a single VLM call, predicting progress without decoupling or success-criteria reasoning. GVL [11] prompts a VLM with temporally shuffled frames, forcing it to judge each frame’s intrinsic progress independently of chronological order to counter the VLM’s bias toward time continuity. TOPReward [12] prompts a VLM with the full video and instruction and, rather than emitting progress as text, extracts it from the token logit of the “True” response to whether the instruction matches the execution. For fair comparison, we select comparable models for TOPReward (Qwen-VL 8B) and GVL (Gemini 3 Flash), and report their scaling performance on better models in Fig. 8 for (Q3).

(Q1) Is D&A an effective reward model for real-world offline and online RL?

Online RL. We apply DSRL [38] to the π0\pi_{0} [46] policy fine-tuned on DROID [47], using the D&A progress score directly as the dense reward. We evaluate on “put the fruit in the bowl” in a DROID kitchen setup (Fig. 4, left), where the π0\pi_{0} base model keeps grasping the ice cream cone and initially solves the task only 10%10\% of the time; learning the correct behavior via RL requires rewards that discriminate good from bad state transitions. D&A provides this signal, assigning zero reward to ice-cream-cone trajectories and high, dense reward for manipulating the banana, raising the success rate to 𝟏𝟎𝟎%\mathbf{100\%} in ∼90{\sim}90 minutes of wallclock time. In contrast, TOPReward assigns high reward to both successful and failed trajectories, leaving success at only 5%5\%.

Offline RL. We condition π0.5\pi_{0.5} [48] on advantages computed from D&A rewards via CFGRL/RECAP [40, 27], centering returns against a global value baseline estimated over the full dataset so that advantages rank state-action pairs against the dataset-wide distribution of outcomes. We collect 50 optimal, 50 suboptimal, and 50 failure demonstrations on a bimanual YAM (Fig. 4) for the task “move the red book from the top shelf to the gray box”, where failures include using the wrong box or arm, or dropping the book mid-transfer. We LoRA-fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} for 50k steps. The baseline π0.5\pi_{0.5} fine-tuned on the successful and suboptimal data only achieves 20%20\% success, reproducing many suboptimal behaviors. TOPReward and Robometer leverage the suboptimal data better, but their noisy rewards fail to fully filter out suboptimality; D&A instead filters these behaviors, improving BC by +𝟖𝟎%\mathbf{+80\%} and outperforming all other models.

Advantage-filtered Behavior Cloning. We collect 50 optimal and 100 suboptimal demonstrations for “nudge out the book ‘Thinking, Fast and Slow’, grasp it, and place it on the table” on a bimanual YAM. Suboptimal demonstrations include nudging or pulling out different books but eventually complete the task. We rank all chunks in the dataset by their advantage AtA_{t} with a single dataset-wide threshold τ\tau, so that chunks are compared against the full distribution of outcomes rather than within their own episode. We LoRA-fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} for 25k steps on the top 35th percentile of chunks (At≥τA_{t}\geq\tau). Robometer and TOPReward both perform poorly, struggling with the long horizon of the task by assigning similar scores to optimal and suboptimal action chunks. Trained on the full dataset, π0.5\pi_{0.5} is competitive but frequently performs suboptimal actions, leading to competitive performance but slow execution. On success, D&A completes the task faster than the baseline fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5}, with 18.8±1.8\mathbf{18.8\pm 1.8} and 28.5±9.228.5\pm 9.2 seconds on average, and with markedly lower variance across rollouts. This shows that D&A filters out suboptimal and retains optimal action chunks.

(Q2) How well does D&A generalize to different tasks and embodiments?

To evaluate D&A across tasks, embodiments, and language, we evaluate on three offline benchmarks: D&A-Bench, a generalization benchmark we collected manually that is guaranteed to be out-of-distribution to all models to stress-test fine-grained scene and language understanding, and two external benchmarks RBM-EVAL-OOD [16] and RoboRewardBenchmark [15]. We propose D&A-Bench to evaluate nuanced scene understanding (e.g., “dose exactly 16 g of coffee beans”), counting (“build a 5 block tower”), and semantic reasoning (“assemble the car”). The benchmark comprises 54 (27 success, 27 failure) trajectories over 14 YAM tasks each annotated with 10 VLM-generated paraphrases of the instruction to test language robustness. We report the Kendall τα\tau_{\alpha} coefficient [49] for D&A-Bench and RBM-EVAL-OOD, measuring how well a reward model’s final-step prediction align with the ground-truth ordering of optimal, sub-optimal, and failure trajectories (∈[−1,+1]\in[-1,+1]; higher is better). RoboRewardBenchmark uses discrete end-of-episode progress labels reports Mean Absolute Error (MAE; lower is better).

Across all three benchmarks (Fig. 5), D&A closes the gap to post-trained models, outperforming RoboReward on RBM-EVAL-OOD, Robometer on RoboRewardBenchmark, and SOLE-R1 on both. On D&A-Bench, D&A leverages the generalization and reasoning capabilities of its base VLM, scoring highest (0.670.67) and beating the best post-trained models Robometer (0.560.56) and RoboReward (0.430.43). Zero-shot TOPReward (0.240.24) and GVL (0.270.27) fail to generalize to those challenging tasks. D&A improves +0.23+0.23 over Naive VLM, which here is a surprisingly strong baseline: because the benchmark rewards scene and language generalization, even unstructured prompting of a strong base VLM generalizes far better than GVL and TOPReward, which cannot reliably compare trajectories. Fig. 7(b) illustrates this on “hit the enter key,” whose completion is only seen by a subtle on-screen change: D&A tracks the full trajectory and cleanly separates the success from a visually similar failure, whereas Robometer assigns the two nearly the same reward, RoboReward/SOLE-R1 score them oppositely, and zero-shot Naive VLM/GVL/TOPReward score both high. More qualitative examples in Sec. XIV. Finally, we demonstrate the scalability of D&A by using GPT-6 Astra as a base model (D&A∗), achieving SOTA results on all three benchmarks.

To evaluate semantic understanding, we plot the confusion matrices between sets of unseen task trajectory videos (rows) and unseen task language instructions (columns) in Fig. 9, where   means the model assigned high and   low reward to the combination. A reward model should discriminate mismatched video–instruction pairs while predicting high reward on the diagonal (correct matches). D&A consistently assigns zero progress to mismatched pairs while accurately scoring correct matches; post-trained models also separate the pairs, whereas zero-shot models cannot, reflecting their bias toward non-zero progress.

(Q3) How does D&A scale with the underlying VLM?

We investigate how D&A’s ability to predict progress from video scales with base model capability. In Fig. 8, we plot trajectory ranking performance (Kendall τα\tau_{\alpha} on RBM-EVAL-OOD) against the cost per million tokens, using cost as a proxy for model capability. Baselines are shown as dashed horizontal lines. Across all base model families, we observe a clear upward trend: as D&A’s base model capability increases, so does the ability to discriminate trajectory optimality. GVL also scales with the underlying model but at a much lower rate. TOPReward faces a major barrier on closed-source models through its reliance on token logprobs—which are unavailable for Gemini 3—and degrading performance under mandatory chat templates enforced by proprietary platforms. Our results further follow the negative scaling trend of TOPReward observed in the original publication [12]. D&A with Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra as a base model achieves SOTA performance on the benchmark with 0.7340.734 and 0.7140.714, validating the observed trend and efficacy of our approach.

To disentangle the base model’s capability from D&A’s gains, we compare Naive VLM and D&A on different base models in Fig. 6(c). On smaller models (Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3.6-Plus), we observe the biggest improvements through D&A, outperforming RoboReward on both benchmarks and Robometer on D&A-Bench. Consequently, D&A enables competitive reward modeling in small open-source and closed-source models. D&A applied to GPT-6 Astra leads to smaller but still substantial gains in reward modeling capabilities. Qualitative examples in Sec. X.

(Q4) What components contribute to D&A’s performance?

To understand how each design decision contributes to the performance of D&A, we perform a series of ablations in Tab. I using Gemini 3.7 Flash. Introducing an explicit success criterion to Naive VLM improves performance by +0.18+0.18 and closes the gap between zero-shot and post-trained methods. Combining the success criteria with decoupling the description and assessment stages, negatively impacts performance due to task-relevant objects not being identifiable or being missing completely from the language description. When grounding the description in the objects present in the video, the performance improves by +0.26+0.26 over the Naive VLM, outperforming post-trained models in some cases.

(Q5) Can rich feedback generated by D&A improve over scalar rewards?

We evaluate D&A as a source of rich feedback to improve Code-as-Policies (CaP) [37] on the LIBERO benchmark (goal suite) [50]. The CaP planner takes multiple attempts at solving the task, generating code and executing it in the environment. We compare a history of code and binary success to extending it with rich feedback generated by D&A. Allowing CaP to iterate over its solutions by giving it history improves performance from 11.4%11.4\% (no history) to 40.6%40.6\% (history). Adding D&A’s rich language feedback achieves 51.4%51.4\% (p=0.00076p=0.00076 over history baseline), showcasing how rich semantic feedback provides a more effective signal than scalar rewards for downstream refinement. See Fig. 10 for an example of feedback improving the behavior.

VI Limitations and Discussion

In this work, we introduce D&A, a methodology for leveraging frontier models in reward modeling and rich feedback. We counter confirmation bias and address hallucinated success by decoupling description and assessment. We demonstrate the efficacy of D&A on several real-world robotic manipulation tasks. While effective, our approach introduces several limitations. First, it inherits the systemic constraints of off-the-shelf frontier models, including high inference latency, token cost, and restricted context windows. Because these models are typically accessed via closed-source APIs, they introduce stochasticity and limited granular control. They also remain susceptible to occasional semantic hallucinations, which can degrade description fidelity and subsequent reward assessment. Second, the generated reward is bounded by the granularity of natural language descriptions. This poses challenges in domains requiring highly nuanced or continuous reward structures that are difficult to verbalize, such as precise spatial relationships or absolute geometric distances. Despite these challenges, D&A marks a pivotal shift from fine-tuning to zero-shot robotics reward modeling that scales with rapid advances in frontier VLMs.

VII Offline RL via Advantage Conditioning: Full Derivation

We provide the full derivation of the advantage-conditioned offline RL pipeline summarized in Sec. IV-D. Unlike standard behavior cloning (BC) or filtered BC, which are strictly constrained by the average performance of the training data, RL can yield a better-than-demonstrator policy.

Suppose we are provided an offline dataset 𝒟={τn}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\{\tau_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} containing NN trajectories. Each trajectory τα\tau_{\alpha} is a sequence of observations and actions, τ={(o1,a1),(o2,a2),…,(oT,aT)}\tau=\{(o_{1},a_{1}),(o_{2},a_{2}),\dots,(o_{T},a_{T})\}. Recall that we treat the progress scores rt=R(o1:T,l)r_{t}=R(o_{1:T},l) as a potential function and define the step-wise potential-based reward as the temporal difference r~t=rt−rt−1\tilde{r}_{t}=r_{t}-r_{t-1} with r0=0r_{0}=0, which effectively captures the instantaneous rate of task improvement at each step.

Because we operate in an offline setting, we can compute empirical state values and advantages entirely offline without the stability risks or compounding errors of bootstrapping. For any timestep tt within a trajectory τα\tau_{\alpha}, the discounted Monte Carlo return is calculated as Gt=∑k=tTγk−t​r~kG_{t}=\sum_{k=t}^{T}\gamma^{k-t}\tilde{r}_{k}, where γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor. To isolate how much better a specific sequence of actions is relative to the entire dataset, we establish a global value baseline VV as the empirical mean of the discounted Monte Carlo returns across all timesteps and all trajectories in 𝒟\mathcal{D}:

V=1∑n=1NTn​∑n=1N∑t=1TnGt,n.V=\frac{1}{\sum_{n=1}^{N}T_{n}}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{n}}G_{t,n}.

Computing VV over the full dataset (rather than per-trajectory or per-task) lets the resulting advantages rank state-action pairs against the dataset-wide distribution of outcomes, which is what CFGRL conditions on. Using this global baseline, the offline advantage A⁡(st,at)A(s_{t},a_{t}) for each state-action pair is computed as the centered return: A⁡(st,at)=Gt−VA(s_{t},a_{t})=G_{t}-V.

These computed advantages can be directly used for downstream offline RL algorithms. We leverage the CFGRL framework [40] to scale actions or action tokens by training a conditional policy πθ​(at∣st,l,g)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},l,g) alongside an unconditional or baseline variant, utilizing the advantage as an explicit conditioning variable gg during optimization. Following RECAP [27], we adapt this advantage-guided framework directly to a π0.5\pi_{0.5} [48] and optimize the model via a standard supervised log-likelihood objective: ℒ⁡(θ)=−𝔼(st,at,l)∈𝒟​[log⁡πθ​(at∣st,l,g)]\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{(s_{t},a_{t},l)\in\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},l,g)\right].

VIII Online RL via Latent Space Noise Steering: Full Derivation

We provide the full optimization details for the online DSRL pipeline, summarized in Sec. IV-D. Unlike the offline setting, which benefits from static, dataset-wide baseline calculations, online policy learning requires the agent to continually explore and optimize its behavior through active environment interaction. DSRL [38] learns a policy πθ​(w∣s,l)\pi_{\theta}(w\mid s,l) that generates a lower-dimensional latent steering vector or noise variable ww, which is then mapped through the frozen base model to produce the final robot actions, rather than optimizing actions directly in the high-dimensional action space.

Under this paradigm, the agent interacts with the environment online, and the absolute task progress score rt=R1:T(o1:T,l)r_{t}=R_{1:T}(o_{1:T},l) generated by D&A is used directly as the dense environmental reward. To optimize the policy over latent space interactions, we maintain a soft action-value function Qϕ​(s,w,l)Q_{\phi}(s,w,l) and a target state-value network Vψ¯​(s,l)V_{\bar{\psi}}(s,l). The critic parameters ϕ\phi are optimized by minimizing the standard temporal-difference (TD) error:

ℒ⁡(ϕ)=𝔼(st,wt,rt,st+1)∼ℬ​[(Qϕ​(st,wt,l)−(rt+γ​Vψ¯​(st+1,l)))2].\mathcal{L}(\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{(s_{t},w_{t},r_{t},s_{t+1})\sim\mathcal{B}}\left[\Big(Q_{\phi}(s_{t},w_{t},l)-\big(r_{t}+\gamma V_{\bar{\psi}}(s_{t+1},l)\big)\Big)^{2}\right]. (2)

Concurrently, the policy parameters θ\theta are updated to maximize the expected future return from the critic alongside an entropy regularization term:

ℒ⁡(θ)=−𝔼st∼ℬ,wt∼πθ​[Qϕ​(st,wt,l)−α​log⁡πθ​(wt∣st,l)].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{s_{t}\sim\mathcal{B},\,w_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[Q_{\phi}(s_{t},w_{t},l)-\alpha\log\pi_{\theta}(w_{t}\mid s_{t},l)\right]. (3)

By mapping this online optimization loop directly onto the latent noise space of a frozen expert, this framework mitigates catastrophic forgetting and policy collapse, enabling sample-efficient online behavior optimization powered by D&A rewards.

IX Additional Results

X Gains of D&A over Base Model Capabilities - Frontier Models

On smaller models (Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3.6-Plus), we observe the biggest improvements through D&A, outperforming RoboReward on both benchmarks and Robometer on D&A-Bench (Fig. 11(a) and Fig. 11(b)). On more recent VLMs, D&A improves reward modeling capabilities, leading to SOTA results on both benchmarks (Fig. 11(c) and Fig. 11(d)). The only exception is Gemini 4 Argon on RBM-EVAL-OOD, where D&A is on par with Naive VLM. Given D&A’s significant improvement on D&A-Bench, we hypothesize that Gemini 4 Argon was trained on the RBM-EVAL-OOD dataset (Google specifically advertises Gemini 4 Argon as a value function11 1 https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/), diluting the benchmark results and preventing D&A from improving.

Qualitatively, Fig. 12(a) and Fig. 13(a) both show the bias toward task success of Naive VLM even when the task is not completed successfully, while Fig. 12(b) and Fig. 13(b) show D&A’s fine-grained reward assignment.

XI Gains of D&A over Base Model Capabilities - Gemini Model Family

The benefits of D&A persist as the base VLM becomes stronger, achieving consistent gains when improving the underlying Gemini models (Tab. V). Crucially, these gains are not driven by increased test-time compute or reasoning, as reducing test-time compute by switching the thinking level to ”low“ matches results and can even improve performance (Tab. V). Furthermore, baselines are evaluated on their strongest compatible backbones—such as Qwen-VL 8B Instruct for TOPReward and Gemini 3 Flash for GVL —rather than artificially weaker models. Existing baselines face major technical barriers on closed-source models: TOPReward relies on token logprobs unavailable on proprietary platforms, GVL performs poorly across closed models, and fine-tuning methods (RoboReward, Robometer) cannot be applied at all. As a result, D&A is the only approach that successfully scales to powerful closed-source models.

XII D&A Cost, Wall Clock Time, and Token Usage

XIII CaP Experiment Details

We evaluate D&A as a between-attempt feedback source for an open-loop code-as-policies planner on the LIBERO libero_goal suite [50]. The planner (gemini-3.7-flash, reasoning effort MEDIUM) observes the initial scene state and generates a code plan of absolute-waypoint primitives (move_to [x,y,z(,g)], gripper, done, ≤40\leq 40 actions) which is then executed open-loop. Each of the 500 initial conditions (10 tasks, 50 initial states each) is attempted 25 times. If required, D&A scores each video (gemini-3.7-flash, reasoning effort MEDIUM, agentview rendered at 448×448448\times 448, downsampled to 16 frames), and its output is appended to the planner’s accumulated history for the next attempt. Let si​(t)∈{0,1}s_{i}(t)\in\{0,1\} denote ground-truth task success of initial condition ii on attempt tt, for i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N (N=500N=500) and t=1,…,25t=1,\dots,25. We report Success@k, cumulative unique initial conditions solved at attempt kk: M⁡(k)=1N​∑i=1Nmax1≤t≤k⁡si​(t)M(k)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\max_{1\leq t\leq k}s_{i}(t)

XIV D&A-Bench Benchmark and Qualitative Results

Dataset: 14 real-world manipulation tasks manually collected on a bimanual YAM robot platform. Each task recorded as 2-4 iPhone-captured episodes (2 success, 2 failure; book task only 1 each), resized to 1280x720. Every task has one handwritten instruction plus 9 AI-generated paraphrases (Gemini 3 Flash, shown first frame of episode + original instruction, prompted for M paraphrases preserving meaning but varying phrasing/specificity/vocabulary), giving 10 instructions/task. Full grid: 14 tasks × 4 episodes × 10 instructions = 560 (episode, instruction) pairs scored per reward model. Below shows predictions of all model for the vanilla instruction. While RBM-OOD-EVAL subsamples the videos to 8 frames [16], we subsample the videos by a factor of 60 (min 8 frames) to capture visual subtleties in the examples below. We make the dataset publicly available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/memmelma/dnabench

XV-B4 Success Criteria and Assessment - Modified for RoboRewardBenchmark

⬇
Task:
"{{task}}"
Scene descriptions:
{{description}}
Given the task instruction and a description of the robot’s rollout video (or the final frame observation), assign a discrete progress score reward (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) for the robot’s performance. Judge only the final state without considering time limits.
Rubric for End-of-Episode Progress:
* 1 - No Success: The final state shows no goal-relevant change for the command.
* 2 - Minimal Progress: The final state shows a small but insufficient change toward the goal.
* 3 - Partial Completion: The final state shows good progress toward the goal but violates more than one requirement or a major requirement.
* 4 - Near Completion: The final state is correct in region and intent but misses a single minor requirement.
* 5 - Perfect Completion: The final state visibly satisfies all requirements.
Hints & Clarifications for Scoring (Particularly 3 vs. 4):
To correctly distinguish between a Partial Completion (3) and a Near Completion (4), you must differentiate between MAJOR and MINOR task requirements based on the following rules:
* Treat a requirement as MAJOR when the PRIMARY object identity or the PRIMARY spatial relation to the reference object is not satisfied. If a major requirement is missed, the score must be 3 or lower.
* Treat a requirement as MINOR when the PRIMARY object identity and PRIMARY spatial relation to the reference object are satisfied, but an AUXILIARY constraint is missed (e.g., the orientation of the object is slightly off, or the object is placed a bit too far forward/backward but still in the correct general region). Missing a single minor requirement results in a score of 4.
Provide a brief step-by-step reasoning analyzing the observation against the rubric and hints. Conclude with your final discrete score in the following JSON format:
[
{{
"score": int
}}
]

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.

We gratefully acknowledge support from our major funders, member institutions, , and all contributors.
